summary: The note describes a city Parks and Recreation initiative offering free outdoor yoga, bootcamp and meditation classes in local parks to promote physical and mental wellbeing. It profiles instructors Sarah Thompson, Mark Daniels and David Greene, plus participant Anna Peterson and psychologist Dr. Emily Pearson, who endorse the mental health benefits. The classes are inclusive, require no fees or equipment, and build community through shared movement and silence.
one_line: A city Parks and Recreation initiative offers free outdoor yoga, bootcamp and meditation classes that support mental health and community.
key_facts: The city's Parks and Recreation department launched outdoor yoga and fitness classes to promote public health and wellness; the article is set on September 5, 2023 at Meadowlark Park.
Sarah Thompson, a certified yoga instructor, leads "Yoga in the Park" every Tuesday and Thursday since September began, at Eastwood Park.
Thompson says that outdoors "our senses are stimulated differently" and that the experience is "inherently meditative."
Mark Daniels, a fitness instructor, has led "Bootcamp in the Park" at Liberty Green every Saturday morning since September 9.
Daniels designs inclusive workouts with modifications so everyone feels welcome, and sees exercise in a shared space as a tool for mental health.
Clinical psychologist Dr. Emily Pearson refers patients to park-based classes and reports significant improvement in mood and reduction in anxiety.
"Meditation Under the Stars" is led by local spiritual coach David Greene at Whispering Pine Park at 7:00 PM on the second Wednesday of each month.
Greene says many fear silence, equating it with loneliness, but the group shares an unspoken understanding of supporting one another by being present.
Anna Peterson, a 56-year-old librarian, joined the yoga classes after a mild depression and calls them a "game-changer."
The classes are open regardless of age, fitness level or exercise experience.
There are no membership fees or expensive equipment requirements; attendees only complete a simple online registration.
The article frames the initiative as reflecting a broader societal shift in attitudes toward mental health, echoing "Healthy mind, healthy body."
